cards.back: Each original strand separates and acts as a **template**. Free nucleotides pair with its exposed bases, so each new DNA molecule contains one original strand and one newly made strand.
cards.hint: Think about what each new molecule keeps from the original.

cards.front: Why can the base sequence of one DNA strand be used to make a new strand?
cards.back: Because of **complementary base pairing**: adenine pairs with thymine and guanine with cytosine. Each template base determines which free nucleotide joins it.

cards.front: Why can DNA polymerase only add nucleotides in one direction?
cards.back: It adds nucleotides only to the **3′ end** of a growing strand, so new DNA is always made 5′ to 3′. It also needs a primer as a starting point.
cards.hint: Consider which end of the growing strand is free.

cards.front: What does helicase do at the replication fork?
cards.back: **Helicase** unwinds the double helix and separates the two strands by breaking hydrogen bonds between paired bases.
cards.hint: Think about what breaks and what it separates.

cards.front: What is the role of primase, and why is it needed?
cards.back: **Primase** makes short RNA primers, which give DNA polymerase a starting point for synthesis.

cards.front: Outline the order in which the enzymes act when DNA is copied.
cards.back: Helicase separates the strands; primase lays RNA primers; DNA polymerase extends them with DNA; the primers are replaced with DNA; **DNA ligase** seals the breaks.

cards.front: How does the leading strand grow?
cards.back: **Continuously** towards the moving replication fork, as DNA polymerase extends it when more template becomes exposed.
cards.hint: Compare this with the lagging strand.

cards.back: A short piece of newly synthesised DNA on the **lagging strand**, made by extending a primer. DNA ligase later joins the fragments together.

cards.front: A student says semi-conservative replication leaves one DNA molecule completely unchanged. What is wrong?
cards.back: That is incorrect. **Semi-conservative** means each resulting molecule contains one original strand and one newly made strand.
cards.hint: Count the strands in each new molecule.

cards.front: A student says the lagging strand grows 3′ to 5′ because it runs away from the fork. What is wrong?
cards.back: Growth direction is not the same as fork direction. Both new strands grow **5′ to 3′**; the lagging strand differs because it is made discontinuously in short pieces.
cards.hint: Check what the note says about direction.

cards.front: Why are RNA primers needed during DNA replication?
cards.back: DNA polymerase cannot start a new strand without a starting point. An **RNA primer** provides an end that DNA polymerase can extend.

cards.front: A student says DNA ligase copies the template strand. What is wrong?
cards.back: Ligase does not copy DNA. It **seals breaks** between adjacent DNA pieces by joining their sugar–phosphate backbones. DNA polymerase adds the nucleotides.

cards.front: Why can the two DNA strands separate without their backbones breaking?
cards.back: The **hydrogen bonds** between paired bases break, while the sugar–phosphate backbones stay intact, so the strands can separate.
